# Study information

## Title

A mixed meta-analysis of future self-continuity and health behaviours

## Authorship

- Fuschia Sirois
- Cormac Monaghan

# Review methods

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## {{< fa circle-question >}}  OSF question

In this section, you register the general type, background and goals of your
review.
:::

## Type of review

The results from this systematic review will be combined with those obtained
from the authors’ labs to form a mixed meta-analysis of own data (MOD) that will
provide a robust and comprehensive psychometric meta-analysis of the
associations between future self-continuity (FSC) and health behaviours.

A clear advantage of this mixed meta-analysis approach is that it can increase
the number of studies to be meta-analysed, which can provide an opportunity for
more robust estimates of the effects, as well as more reliable moderator
analyses. Including studies from outside of the authors’ labs also helps to
reduce any potential biases in the analysis.

## Review stages

As it is expected that there will be limited research on our target variables,
future self-continuity (FSC) and health behaviours, the Review stages are basic:

Search, Screening, Extraction, Synthesis with studies garnered from the
systematic search and those from existing data sets from the authors’ labs.

## Current review stage

The full literature search and screening has yet to be conducted.

Data sets from the authors’ labs have been identified but not analysed.

## Start date

The planned start date is **August 26, 2026**

## End date

The estimated end date for when the results from this systematic search are
retrieved and combined with those from existing data sets is September 30, 2026.

# Background

This meta-analysis seeks to quantify the association between future
self-continuity (FSC) and health behaviours, as well as examine the factors that
may attenuate or strengthen this association.

Previous meta-analyses have demonstrated the value of future-oriented thinking
for self-regulation more generally, and the regulation of health behaviours more
specifically (Baird et al., 2021). An emerging evidence base also links future
self-continuity (FSC) more specifically to the practice of a range of health
promoting behaviours. Feeling closer to one’s future self can heighten the
saliency of the distal outcomes that arise from engaging in current health
behaviours, and therefore facilitate better engagement.

Yet we know little about the magnitude of this association or the factors that
might attenuate or amplify this association. There are also now a number of
interventions shown to increase FSC, making it a reasonable target for
intervention to increase health-promoting behaviours,

Gaining a clearer understanding of the association between FSC and health
behaviours is crucial to help inform potential interventions aimed at improving
the practice of health promoting behaviours by increasing identification with
and felt closeness to the Future Self. Identifying the facilitators and barriers
involved (aka moderators) can also provide valuable knowledge for more targeted
approaches to improve health behaviours via bolstering FSC.

Additionally, we will explore the potential contributions of future self-rated
health (SRH) in the proposed link between FSC and health behaviours. FSRH
reflects appraisals of future health and may contribute to the motivation to
engage in health behaviours to help achieve the expected future health states.
Expected future health states (i.e., FSRH) may therefore account for possible
shared variance between FSC and health behaviours. To explore this proposition,
we will calculate and then meta-analyse the semi-partial correlations between
FSC and health behaviours after accounting for the contributions of FSRH, using
the data sets from our Labs and any published studies that include a measure of
FSRH.

This meta-analysis will provide essential knowledge to meet these goals by
combining data from a systematic search of the research literature with data
gathered from the author's labs. Taking this combined or mixed meta-analysis
approach will provide the critical mass needed to conduct a more robust
meta-analysis as well as moderator analyses to probe the sources of variability
in the effects.

## Research Questions

### Primary research question

To what extent is FSC associated with the practice of health-promoting
behaviours? To what extent does future self-rated health (FSRH) account for this
association?

### Secondary research question

What factors (e.g., sample characteristics, methodological factors) influence
the association between FSC and health-promoting behaviours?

## Expectations / hypotheses

It is expected that FSC will be positively associated with health-promoting
behaviours. I is also expected that when the shared variance from FSRH is
accounted for, the association between FSC and health behaviours will be
attenuated.

## Dependent variable(s)

Health-promoting/healthy behaviours will be considered the outcome variable for
the purposes of this meta-analysis. Health-promoting behaviours will include
healthy eating/diet behaviours, physical exercise/activity, and sleep-related
behaviours. Safety and preventive health behaviours (i.e., seat belt use,
screening behaviours), and health risky behaviors (disordered eating, substance
and alcohol misuse, sexual health behaviours, etc.) will be excluded as these
form separate dimensions of health-related behaviors to those included under the
umbrella of health-promoting behavior.

## Independent variable(s)

FSC will be considered the independent variable for the purposes of this
meta-analysis.

## Additional variable(s) / covariate(s)

We will examine whether sample characteristics (participant age, sex, and
whether the sample is student, adult, or medical/clinical) and the nature of the
scale used (type of FSC scale, single item or multi-item measure; single health
behaviour or summary measure of health behaviours) moderate the associations
between FSC and health behaviours. We will also examine the contribution of FSRH
to the association between FSC and health-promoting behaviours. Software

Endnote will be used to store and screen search results. Excel will be used for
initial extraction and data checking. R (Version 4.6.0) will be used to
synthesise the results.

## Funding

This project is unfunded.

## Conflicts of interest

There are no conflicts of interest to declare.

## Overlapping authorships

The lead author on this project is an active researcher in the areas of future
oriented thinking and health behaviours, and data sets from their lab will be
included as part of the MOD analysis. However, neither author have published
work on the link between FSC and health behaviours.

# Search Strategy

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## {{< fa circle-question >}}  OSF question

In this section, you register your search strategy: the procedures you designed
to obtain all (potentially) relevant sources to review (e.g., articles, books,
preprints, reports, case law, policy papers, archived documents).
:::

## Databases

Web of Science, Scopus, PsyArXiv, and PsychINFO, and supplemented with a filter
search of the first 20 pages of Google Scholar. Interfaces

The Discover interface will be used to search the Web of Science, Scopus, and
PsychINFO. The internet will be used to search Google Scholar Grey literature

Google Scholar will be used to search the grey literature, as will PsyArXiv.

## Inclusion and exclusion criteria

**Inclusion criteria:** Papers and articles in full text, English language with
adult populations (age 18 or over) that study the relationship between FSC and
health behaviours will be included. Papers and articles can report research with
both clinical or non-clinical populations and must report unique effects not
reported in other published papers, reports, theses or conference papers. In
such instances the effect from the most recent and complete source will be used
for the meta-analysis.

**Exclusion criteria:** Any review papers, papers and articles where full text
cannot be obtained, and any papers including child or non-adult populations will
be excluded from this meta-analysis. Additionally, any papers or articles not
using appropriate or valid measures of FSC or health-promoting behaviors (as
defined above) will be excluded.

No framework was used to inform the search strategy as we are searching for
associations between two variables across multiple populations and not
intervention effects. Query strings

Query strings to run (from 2009, when the first measure of FSC was published by
Ersner-Herschfield and colleagues). The strings will use MeSH terms to expand
the search.

- future self-continuity\*
- AND health behaviour\* OR Diet, healthy OR physical activity\* OR physical
  exercise\* OR sleep\*

## Search validation procedure

No search validation procedure will be used as this is a basic search.

## Other search strategies

All articles garnered from the search strategies will be further checked via
forward and backward search strategies to identify any additional papers for
inclusion.

## Procedures to contact authors

If essential data are not reported, we will contact authors via email requesting
this information and allow a 2-week response window. If there is no response,
then that study will not be included in the analysis.

## Results of contacting authors

We will report the number of authors contacted and the response rate in the
written report of the meta-analysis.

## Search expiration and repetition

We do not expect that the literature on this topic will expand, as it is a
fairly niche topic. Accordingly, no repeat of the search is planned. Search
strategy justification

The association of FSC with health behaviours is a very niche topic. The search
strategies and contact procedures detailed above reflect this consideration and
are therefore very basic.

## Miscellaneous search strategy details

None.

# Screening

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## {{< fa circle-question >}}  OSF question

In this section, you register your screening procedure: the procedure you
designed to eliminate all irrelevant sources from the results of the search
strategy (and retain the relevant sources).
:::

## Screening stages

- **Stage 1:** Title screening for identifying duplicates, papers focused on a
  relevant topic, and paper language.
- **Stage 2:** Abstract screening for assessing other eligibility criteria
- **Stage 3:** Full text screening for useable data

All screening will be conducted by a human

## Screened fields / blinding

All bibliographic fields will be visible during the screening.

## Used exclusion criteria

Studies will be excluded if:

- They are reviews and do not report primary data
- They do not analyse the association of FSC with a measure of a
  health-promoting behaviors.
- If necessary data is not reported and cannot be obtained from the authors
- If they report data already reported in another paper; In such instances the
  effect from the most recent and complete source will be used for the
  meta-analysis.

## Screening reliability

For Stage 1 the first screener will conduct the full screening alone if \>100
papers are retrieved for screening, with 20% of these checked by the second
screener. If there are \<100 papers retrieved, then both the first and second
screener will conduct the Stage 1 screening.

Both the first and second screener will conduct the screening for Stage 2 and 3
screening stages. Screening will be conducted independently and decisions
recorded in separate Excel files.

## Screening reconciliation procedure

Discrepancies will be resolved by the project PI.

## Sampling and sample size

Not applicable as this systematic search will be used to supplement a
meta-analysis of existing data sets reporting the association of FSC with health
behaviours. Screening procedure justification

This is a small-scale search on a niche topic that will supplement a
meta-analysis of existing data sets.

## Data management and sharing

Given this is a small-scale search that will supplement the analysis for the
larger project, no detailed information about the sources will be reported or
shared. The basic reporting of number of studies retrieved from the searches and
screened out at each stage (with reasons) will be reported in the PRISMA
diagram.

## Miscellaneous screening details

Not applicable.

## Entities to extract

Entities to be extracted:

- Estimations of associations between variables or effect sizes: Pearson’s r.
- Independent and dependent variable descriptives: means, standard deviations.
- FSC scale used, including whether it’s a single item or multi-item scale.
- Type of health behaviour(s) measured, for single behaviour measures.
- Single health behaviour measure or summary health behaviour measure.
- Sample characteristics: Population, sample mean age, percentage female
- Study design
- Country of research
- Study meta-data: Authors, year of publication/report, publication type
  (published vs type of unpublished)

## Extraction stages

Extraction stages:

- **Stage 1 - Training stage:** The primary extractor and second extractor are
  given instruction on the extraction procedure, where to locate data, and a
  trial supervised extraction.
- **Stage 2 - Primary data extraction:** Main extractor and second extractor
  will extract primary data and record it in an excel file independently, and in
  parallel.
- **Stage 3 – Reliability verification stage:** Project PI will check both
  extractions and any discrepancies will be resolved through discussion.

## Extractor masking

No extractor masking will be used as this is a small-scale review of a niche
area.

## Extraction reliability

No extractor masking will be used as this is a small-scale review of a niche
area.

## Extraction reconciliation procedure

Both extractors will conduct their extraction in parallel using separate Excel
files to ensure independence.

## Extraction procedure justification

Given this is a small-scale systematic search of a niche research topic, it is
expected that number of eligible studies retrieved will be relatively small. As

# Synthesis and Quality Assessment

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}
## {{< fa circle-question >}}  OSF question

In this section, you register the procedure for the review’s synthesis: the
procedure you designed to use the data that was extracted from each source to
answer your research question(s). This often includes transforming the raw
extracted data, verifying validity, applying predefined inference criteria,
interpreting results, and presenting results. Additionally, you register
procedures you designed to assess bias in individual sources and the synthesis
itself.
:::

## Planned data transformations

Bivariate correlations will be used to calculate the partial correlations
between FSC and health-promoting behaviours, partialing out the contribution of
FSRH.

If needed, effects will be converted to a common metric prior to analysis, which
is expected to be a Pearson’s r. However, given the focus of the review it is
expected that most effects will be in a Pearson’s r value.

The percent female participants in each study will be transformed into a decimal
figure (i.e., 71% as 0.71) so that it can be treated as a continuous moderator
in the overall meta-regression analyses that will combine the results of this
search with data from the author’s own data sets. Missing data

Studies with missing essential data (i.e., Pearson r values) that cannot be
retrieved by contacting the authors will be excluded from the analyses. Data
validation

If a study reports Pearson r values for the association of FSC with health
behaviours that are moderate to large but in the opposite of the expected
direction authors will be contacted to verify whether the value is correct. If
this strategy does not work, we will review any reported associations of each of
these focal variables with other variables to verify of the directions with
those variables (triangulation) are in the expected direction. If these other
associations are also not in the expected direction(s) and we cannot reach the
authors to verify the data’s validity, then we will remove this study as the
data are likely not valid. If the correlations with other variables is in the
expected direction, we will identify this study as an outlier and conduct a
sensitivity analysis to determine its effect on the overall pooled effect size.

## Quality assessment

Risk of bias for correlational studies will be assessed using a bespoke quality
tool created from existing or previously used quality tools and following the
recommendations of Quintana (2015) and the applicable appraisal criteria
suggested by the Joanna Briggs Institute Checklist for Analytical
Cross-Sectional Studies. Aspects of the study quality including sampling
strategy, representativeness of the sample, sample size, clarity of the
hypotheses and methods used, and appropriateness of the analyses will be
considered. Two independent reviewers will be involved in the quality assessment
and interrater reliability will be assessed using Cohen’s Kappa. Note that this
tool will only be used to assess the published studies garnered from the
searches.

## Synthesis plan

Data retrieved from this search will be combined with the authors’ existing data
sets from both published and unpublished studies to form a mixed meta-analysis.
All analysis will be conducted in R (version 4.6.0) using a combination of the
metafor (Viechtbauer, 2010) and meta (Balduzzi et al., 2019) packages.

The primary analysis will consist of a random-effects meta-analysis to estimate
the overall association between FSC and health-promoting behaviors.
Random-effects models will be estimated using restricted maximum likelihood.

FSC will be examined as the primary predictor in the random-effects
meta-analysis to estimate the magnitude of the association with the practice of
health-promoting behaviors. When there is more than one time point, the effects
at baseline will be used.

The secondary analysis will consists of a meta-analysis of the partial
correlations between FSC and health-promoting behaviours, accounting for the
contributions of FSRH.

Statistical heterogeneity will be quantified using the Q statistic (Card, 2012),
the between study variance (τ\^2) and the I\^2 statistic (Higgins & Thompson,
2002). If the Q statistic is associated with a large confidence interval, and
the I-square values are \> 50 percent (reflecting moderate heterogeneity) (Card,
2012), then moderator analyses will be conducted if viable.

Moderator analyses will only be undertaken when sufficient data are available to
permit reliable estimation. For categorical moderators, three or more samples
per subgroup are necessary, as suggested by Card (2012). For continuous
moderators, a minimum of 10 samples is necessary for a meta-regression, as
suggested by the Cochrane collaboration.

Moderation analysis for categorical moderators (i.e., single vs multi item FSC
scale; single vs multiple-health behaviour measure) will be conducted using
subgroup analysis. Individual levels of heterogeneity with each subgroup will
also be reported. Moderation analysis for continuous moderators (sample mean
age, percentage female in sample) will be conducted using meta-regression to
assess the potential influence percentage of females on the overall effects. If
planned moderator analyses cannot be conducted because of an insufficient number
of studies or inadequate reporting, these analyses will be omitted and the
reasons documented. In such cases, the review will focus on descriptive
summaries of study characteristics alongside the primary random-effects
meta-analysis.

## Criteria for conclusions / inference criteria

We will use the standard p \< .05 criteria for determining whether the average
effect size from the meta-analysis is statistically significant, and whether the
moderator analyses are significant.

## Synthesist blinding

There will be no blinding of the synthesis given the nature of this review
(supplement to meta-analysis of existing data sets).

## Synthesis reliability

One synthesist will be involved.

## Synthesis reconciliation procedure

Not applicable.

## Publication bias analyses

We will assess publication bias and small-study effects using a multi-pronged
approach via the metafor package (Viechtbauer, 2010).

Visual inspection of contour-enhanced funnel plots will first be undertaken to
assess the presence of asymmetry. Funnel plot asymmetry will be formally
evaluated using Egger's regression test (Egger et al. 1997). To examine the
potential impact of publication bias on the pooled estimates, Duval and
Tweedie's (2000) trim-and-fill procedure will be conducted.

In addition, publication bias will be examined using selection models (Carter et
al., 2019). Where model convergence and the number of included studies permit,
results from the selection model will be compared with the primary
random-effects analysis to evaluate the robustness of the conclusions to
potential publication bias.

## Sensitivity analyses / robustness checks

Sensitivity analyses will be performed should any study include methods that are
different from the majority of the studies included, for example, use of a study
design that is not similar to the majority of the studies.

Because we will be combining the data from studies identified through a
systematic literature search with data from our own labs, we will conduct a
robustness check by evaluating any influence of data source (search vs lab data)
on the results.

## Synthesis procedure justification

Random effects meta-analysis is standard for summarising correlations across
diverse samples. Other decisions regarding data integrity, missing data, and
inference criteria are reasonable given the small scale of this review and its
purpose to supplement data from the authors' labs.

## Synthesis data management and sharing

An Excel file with the data extraction will be made available on the project osf
site after the embargo period. R Scripts will also be made available.

## Miscellaneous synthesis details

Risk for bias due to the inclusion of data sets from the authors’ labs will be
tested by comparing the effect sizes garnered from the published literature to
those obtained from the data sets from the authors’ labs via categorical
moderation test
